# Summative challenge: herbicide, light & interacting stressors

This brings the whole day together. You will build and fit a model that combines **everything**: two categorical factors, an **interaction** between them, random effects for an experimental grouping variable, and the full diagnostic and model-checking workflow.

## The scenario

Marine microalgae are the base of the coastal food web, and they face several pressures at once. Runoff from farmland carries the herbicide **diuron** onto inshore reefs, where it blocks photosynthesis. At the same time, sediment in that same runoff makes the water **murkier**, cutting the light reaching the algae.

The obvious question is whether these two stressors simply add up, or whether one changes the effect of the other. That is an **interaction**, and it matters enormously for management: if diuron only does damage under certain light conditions, then where and when you control it changes.

King et al. (2022) ran exactly this experiment on the diatom *Phaeodactylum tricornutum*. Flasks of algae were grown at **three light levels** crossed with **five diuron concentrations** — 15 treatment combinations — and photosynthetic yield was measured after 72 hours. The whole 15-cell experiment was repeated on **four separate occasions**, each with an independent algal culture. Those occasions are the **blocks**.

`algal-yield.csv` has one row per flask (n = 60):

- `yield_ps` — photosynthetic yield, $Y(II)$, measured by chlorophyll-a fluorescence (our response). Higher is healthier; it runs from about 0.24 to 0.59 here.
- `light` — light level as a **factor**: `1` = 5, `2` = 20, `3` = 80 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. Level 1 (lowest light) is the reference.
- `diuron` — diuron concentration as a **factor**: `1` = 0 (control), `2` = 0.11, `3` = 0.33, `4` = 1, `5` = 3 µg L⁻¹. Level 1 (no diuron) is the reference.
- `block` — which of the four algal cultures the flask belonged to. This is the **random-effects grouping variable**.
- `light_umol`, `diuron_ugL` — the original numeric values of the two treatments, in case you want them.

::: callout-important
## Why both stressors are factors, not numbers

It is tempting to drop `light_umol` and `diuron_ugL` straight into the model as continuous predictors. Don't — at least not as your main model. Neither effect is close to linear in its numeric value. Light runs 5 → 20 → 80, and yield falls sharply between 5 and 20 but then barely changes between 20 and 80. A straight line through those three points would miss the pattern entirely.

Treating each as a factor lets every level find its own value, with no assumption about the shape of the dose–response. That is the whole reason the experiment used a small number of carefully chosen levels rather than a continuous gradient.
:::

> **Data & attribution.** King, O.C., van de Merwe, J.P., Campbell, M.D., Smith, R.A., Warne, M.St.J. & Brown, C.J. (2022) *Interactions among multiple stressors vary with exposure duration and biological response.* **Proceedings of the Royal Society B** 289: 20220348. <https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2022.0348>. The course file is the 72-hour slice of the diuron experiment, with the two treatments recoded as factor levels.

## Building the model

Start from the reference coding you met in Module 17 and add the interaction. The response is continuous, so this is a Normal model — no link function needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\texttt{yield\_ps}_i &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i,\ \sigma) \\
\mu_i &= \alpha + \beta^L_{\,\text{light}_i} + \beta^D_{\,\text{diuron}_i} + \beta^{LD}_{\,\text{light}_i}\!\times\!\texttt{diuron\_ugL}_i + b_{\,\text{block}_i} \\
b_j &\sim \text{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_b), \quad \textstyle\sum_j b_j = 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Reading the terms left to right:

- $\alpha$ — mean yield in the **reference cell**: lowest light, no diuron.
- $\beta^L_2,\beta^L_3$ — the effect of medium and high light, relative to low light. $\beta^L_1$ is fixed at 0.
- $\beta^D_2 \ldots \beta^D_5$ — the effect of each diuron dose relative to the control, **at the reference light level**. $\beta^D_1$ is fixed at 0.
- $\beta^{LD}_2,\beta^{LD}_3$ — the **interaction**: how much the diuron effect changes at medium and high light. $\beta^{LD}_1$ is fixed at 0.
- $b_j$ — the block offset, one per algal culture, partially pooled as in Module 19 and constrained to sum to zero (see the tips below — this matters a lot here).

::: callout-note
## A note on how the interaction is written

The diuron **main effects** are fully categorical (one free parameter per dose), but the interaction uses the *numeric* dose `diuron_ugL`. This is a deliberate compromise: a fully categorical interaction would need $2 \times 4 = 8$ extra parameters, and with only four blocks and 60 flasks there is not much information per parameter. Writing the interaction as a light-specific *slope* on dose captures "diuron bites harder at low light" with just two parameters.

If you want to see the fully categorical version, it is a good extension — it fits, and tells the same story with wider intervals.
:::

Fixing a coefficient at zero is done with a deterministic assignment, exactly as you would write any other `<-` line:

```
  bL[1] <- 0
  bL[2] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  bL[3] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
```

## Tips before you fit

::: callout-important
## Centre the prior on $\alpha$ where the data actually are

Everywhere else in this course, `dnorm(0, ...)` has been a perfectly good prior for an intercept, because the response was either on a log/logit scale or roughly centred on zero. **Here it is not.** Yield is a proportion-like quantity that lives between about 0.24 and 0.59 — it is never remotely near zero, and it is never negative.

A prior of `dnorm(0, 1)` on $\alpha$ says "before seeing data, I think mean yield is about 0, and I would not be shocked by −1". That is a statement no one believes. With 60 observations the likelihood will drag $\alpha$ to the right place anyway, but you have made the sampler start in and travel through a region the data strongly reject, which wastes burn-in and can slow mixing.

Centre it on something plausible instead:

```
  alpha ~ dnorm(0.5, 0.5)
```

Mean 0.5, SD 0.5 — comfortably covering every yield value in the dataset and still vague enough to let the data speak. **The general lesson:** a prior's *location* matters as much as its width, and "centred on zero" is a habit, not a rule. Ask what scale your response is on before you write it down.
:::

::: callout-important
## Keep $\sigma_b$ on the scale of the response

Module 20 showed how an over-wide prior wrecks sampling. This model is a live example, and it is the single most likely thing to go wrong here.

Yield varies over a range of about 0.35, and the residual SD is around 0.02. A block SD of 10 is therefore physically impossible — it would mean cultures differing by more than the entire measurement scale. But `sigma.b ~ dunif(0, 10)` declares exactly that to be plausible, and the consequences are severe: with only **four** blocks there is very little information about $\sigma_b$, so the chains follow the prior out to absurd values, the $\alpha$-versus-$b_j$ ridge from Module 20 opens up, and R-hat for the intercept climbs into the **tens**.

Scale the prior to the response:

```
  sigma.b ~ dunif(0, 0.2)
  sigma   ~ dunif(0, 1)
```

Try it both ways if you have time — the broken version is instructive, and diagnosing it from the trace plots alone is exactly the skill Module 20 was building.
:::

::: callout-important
## Pin the block effects down with a sum-to-zero constraint

Even with a well-scaled prior on $\sigma_b$, four blocks is few enough that $\alpha$ and the $b_j$ still trade off against each other — that same Module 20 ridge, narrowed but not closed. Fit the model with the $b_j$ all free and you will likely see R-hat for $\alpha$ **above 5** with an ESS in the single digits, while every fixed effect looks perfect. One chain wanders off with $\sigma_b$ stuck near its upper bound and never comes back.

The cure is to **remove the redundancy** rather than sample through it. Let three block effects be free and define the fourth as minus their sum, so the four offsets are forced to average exactly zero:

```
  b[1] ~ dnorm(0, sigma.b)
  b[2] ~ dnorm(0, sigma.b)
  b[3] ~ dnorm(0, sigma.b)
  b[4] <- -(b[1] + b[2] + b[3])
```

Now $\alpha$ means something unambiguous — the grand mean across blocks — and there is no direction left for the chains to slide along. The effect on the diagnostics is dramatic: R-hat drops from above 5 to **1.01**, and $\sigma_b$'s ESS goes from about 5 to over 800, with no change to any posterior mean. The model fits comfortably at the default sampler settings.

This is the general lesson of Module 20 applied to a real model: when the chains will not mix, respecify the model so the thing you cannot estimate is no longer in it.
:::

::: callout-tip
## Other things worth knowing

- **Set the constants.** The model needs `N` = 60, which FANGS fills in from the data. The sum-to-zero block effects are written out one per line, so you do not need a `J` constant at all — but if you experiment with a free `for (j in 1:J)` version, set `J` = 4 in the Model constants panel.
- **Priors on the fixed effects.** `dnorm(0, 1)` is fine for all the $\beta$ terms — these are *differences* in yield, genuinely centred on zero, and an SD of 1 is very generous for effects that turn out to be around 0.2.
- **Expect $\sigma_b$ to be small.** The blocks turn out to differ very little. A posterior for $\sigma_b$ that piles up near zero is a real result, not a failure — it says the experiment was well controlled.
- **$\alpha$ still has the lowest ESS.** Even with the sum-to-zero constraint, the intercept mixes more slowly than the $\beta$ terms. R-hat near 1.0 with an ESS in the low hundreds is fine; run more samples if you want it tighter.
:::

## Bring your whole toolkit

- **Run a prior predictive check** before fitting (Module 7). With the priors above, are the simulated yields in a believable range?
- After fitting, check **R-hat and ESS** (Module 10) — repair the model if the variance parameters mix badly.
- Run a **posterior predictive check** (Module 9) to confirm the model reproduces the spread of yield values.
- Use the **Joint distribution** tab to look at $\alpha$ against $\sigma_b$. You should see the funnel shape that hierarchical models are famous for.

## Your task

Fit the full model to `algal-yield.csv` and read the **Summary** tab. The answer box below asks for $\alpha$, the two light effects, the highest diuron dose, the two interaction terms, and both SDs — but read the whole table, because the questions below need the lower doses too. Then answer the science questions:

1. **Does diuron reduce photosynthetic yield?** Look at $\beta^D_5$ — the highest dose, 3 µg L⁻¹ — against the control.
2. **Is there a dose–response?** Read $\beta^D_2$ through $\beta^D_5$ in order. Which doses have credible intervals that exclude zero, and which do not?
3. **Does light change the diuron effect?** This is the interaction. If $\beta^{LD}_2$ and $\beta^{LD}_3$ are credibly **positive**, then diuron does *less* damage as light increases — the stressors are **antagonistic**, not simply additive.
4. **How much did blocking matter?** Compare $\sigma_b$ with $\sigma$.

Pass this and you have fit a real hierarchical model with interacting factors, end to end, and drawn a management-relevant conclusion from it. 🎉
